body:
Today's scan turned up zero arbitrage opportunities across the 81 live gold contracts on Kalshi and Polymarket -- a genuinely quiet day rather than a gap in the scanner. Kalshi's threshold ladder (Gold price on September 30, 2026 — Above $X) is priced consistently: the strike nearest breakeven, $4,330.99, sits at 52¢ bid / 56¢ ask, and prices decay smoothly through higher strikes, with no crossed markets between adjacent contracts that a bot could exploit.

The strike prices themselves look extreme only if you haven't been watching gold this year. Gold rose to 4,350.36 USD/t.oz on September 11, 2026, up 0.76% from the previous day, which lines up almost exactly with where Kalshi's above contracts flip from favoring yes to favoring no. The World Gold Council reported on September 9 that global gold-backed ETFs took in $18 billion in August, the second-largest monthly inflow on record, with holdings rising 121 tonnes to an all-time high of 4,189 tonnes. That kind of inflow, plus PPI data pushing September rate-hike odds to roughly 60%, up from August's 31% low, explains why both platforms are pricing meaningful odds on strikes as high as $4,900-$5,500 by year end -- it reflects a real, well-documented rally, not a data error.

One thing worth flagging for readers: Kalshi's contracts settle on the spot price at a fixed date, while Polymarket's touch contracts (e.g., hit $4,300 in September) pay out if the intraday price ever reaches that level, resolving differently even against the same underlying. That structural difference is a common source of apparent mispricing between the two platforms and is worth remembering before reading too much into any single price gap.
headline: No arbitrage found across 81 gold contracts on Kalshi and Polymarket
